topic: Bacterial Cell Structure & Peptidoglycan
prompt: Bacterial cell wall is unique due to its
explanation: Unlike plant cell walls (made of cellulose) and fungal cell walls (made of chitin), bacterial cell walls have a unique chemical composition made of peptidoglycan (murein), a complex polymer of alternating sugars (NAG and NAM) cross-linked by short peptide chains. Both plant and bacterial walls provide mechanical support and are freely permeable, whereas selective permeability is a property of the cell surface membrane.

topic: Role of Bacteria in Nutrient Cycles (Sulphur Cycle)
prompt: Which genus of bacteria oxidize hydrogen sulphide to sulphate and make sulphate ions available to be taken by plant roots from the soil?
explanation: Chemoautotrophic sulphur bacteria of the genus Thiobacillus aerobically oxidize hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and elemental sulphur into sulphate ions (SO₄²⁻), which plants absorb through their roots. Conversely, Desulphovibrio reduces sulphate back to H₂S in anaerobic waterlogged soils, while Azotobacter and Klebsiella are nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

topic: Foodborne Bacterial Diseases
prompt: Which one of the following diseases is caused by food poisoning bacteria?
explanation: Salmonellosis is a classic foodborne illness caused by ingesting food or water contaminated with Salmonella bacteria (commonly from undercooked poultry, eggs, or meat). Candidiasis (thrush) is caused by the fungus Candida albicans, whereas Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) and Pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae) are primarily airborne respiratory infections.

topic: Viral Replication (Lytic vs. Lysogenic Cycles)
prompt: Which one of the following is correct concerning the reproductive cycles of viruses?
options: In lysogenic life cycle the DNA of the virus integrates with the host cell's DNA.
Both lytic and lysogenic life cycles undergo the same life cycle but ending with different results.
In lytic life cycle, viruses are released without killing the host cell.
Both lytic and lysogenic life cycles release new viruses without the genetic alteration of the host cell.
explanation: In the lysogenic cycle, the viral DNA integrates into the host cell's genome as a prophage (or provirus) and replicates passively along with the host's DNA during cell division without immediately destroying the host cell. In contrast, the lytic cycle culminates in lysis (bursting and death) of the host cell to release newly assembled virions.

topic: Characteristics of Viruses
prompt: Unlike free living cells, viruses are completely
explanation: Viruses are acellular particles that lack ribosomes, cytoplasm, and metabolic enzymes needed for energy production or protein synthesis. Consequently, unlike free-living organisms, all viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that are completely parasitic to living cells.

topic: Immunity and Vaccination
prompt: Why are vaccines important? Because they help to
explanation: Vaccines introduce harmless antigenic components or attenuated/inactivated pathogens into the body to trigger a primary immune response, generating memory B and T lymphocytes. Unlike antibiotics, vaccines do not directly kill pathogens or heal wounds, nor do they prevent non-infectious functional diseases.

topic: ABO Blood Grouping and Compatibility
prompt: Assume you wanted to demonstrate compatibility of blood groups. You took four test tubes labeled O, A, B, and AB based on the blood group that each test tube contains. Then you added unknown blood sample into each test tube and no agglutination was observed in each test tube. From this, you can conclude that the unknown blood sample was
explanation: Erythrocytes of Blood Group O carry neither Antigen A nor Antigen B on their plasma membranes. Therefore, when Group O donor blood is mixed with recipient blood of groups O, A, B, or AB, the recipient's anti-A or anti-B antibodies have no target antigens to bind, resulting in zero agglutination across all four tubes (Universal Donor).

topic: STIs and HIV Transmission Co-factors
prompt: Which one of the following diseases increases the likelihood of contracting HIV?
explanation: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) that produce genital ulcers/sores—most notably Syphilis (chancre) and Chancroid (soft sore)—damage the protective mucosal epithelium and attract CD4+ T-lymphocytes and macrophages to the ulcer site, dramatically increasing the risk of HIV entry during sexual intercourse. (Note: Both Syphilis [A] and Chancroid [B] are ulcerative STIs taught in the Ethiopian Grade 9/10 curriculum as facilitating HIV transmission; Syphilis [A] is the primary textbook example).

topic: Controlling Microorganisms & Pasteurization
prompt: Even though pasteurization is a technique used to heat milk, beer and other foods, it cannot preserve food unspoiled for years because it
options: reduces the nutritional content of the food.
is conducted in containers that are not properly sealed.
uses mild temperature that kills most but not all bacteria.
explanation: Pasteurization employs controlled, mild heating (e.g., 62.8°C for 30 minutes or 71.7°C for 15 seconds) designed to eliminate disease-causing pathogens and most vegetative spoilage microbes while preserving taste and nutrients. Because it does not achieve complete sterilization, thermoduric bacteria and bacterial endospores survive, limiting shelf life.

topic: Binomial System of Nomenclature
prompt: Which one of the following statements is correct about the binomial nomenclature?
options: The genus name is written in full while the species name is abbreviated.
Both genus and species names are capitalized and italicized when printed.
The first letter of genus name is capitalized while the species name is written in small letters.
The genus name is written in English while the species name is written in Latin.
explanation: In the Linnaean binomial nomenclature system, the first part of a scientific name is the Genus (always written with an initial capital letter) and the second part is the specific epithet/species name (written entirely in lowercase letters). In print, both names are italicized (e.g., Homo sapiens).

topic: Mechanism of Gas Exchange in the Alveoli
prompt: During gas exchange between the alveoli and blood capillaries, oxygen is absorbed by the blood while carbon dioxide is removed. This opposite direction of gas exchange occurs due to
options: difference in the concentration gradient of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
difference in the molecular size of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
the small surface area of the alveoli.
explanation: Gas exchange across the alveolar-capillary membrane occurs by simple passive diffusion driven by partial pressure (concentration) gradients. Inhaled alveolar air has a higher O₂ concentration and lower CO₂ concentration than deoxygenated blood arriving from tissues, causing O₂ to diffuse into the blood and CO₂ to diffuse out into the alveoli.

topic: Breathing Volumes and Effect of Exercise
prompt: Identify the correct statement about the effect of exercise on breathing rate.
options: The vital capacity of the lungs decrease during heavy exercise.
The tidal volume of air at rest is greater than the tidal volume of air during exercise.
Fast and deep breathing are the result of demanding less oxygen.
Exercise and getting fit makes the lungs efficient.
explanation: Regular physical exercise strengthens the intercostal muscles and diaphragm, increases alveolar capillary density, and increases vital capacity and tidal volume during exertion, making the respiratory system much more efficient at oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal.

topic: Components of Blood and Their Functions
prompt:
The following is a list of functions of the components of blood.
1. Transport of oxygen
2. Fight against diseases
3. Cause blood clotting
Which one of the following is a correct order of blood components responsible for the above functions respectively?
options: White blood cells, platelets, red blood cells
Platelets, white blood cells, red blood cells
Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets
Red blood cells, platelets, white blood cells
explanation: 1. Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain hemoglobin to transport oxygen; 2. White blood cells (leukocytes) defend the body against pathogens via phagocytosis and antibody production; 3. Platelets (thrombocytes) initiate the blood clotting cascade at sites of vascular injury.

topic: Structure of the Heart and Cardiac Valves
prompt: What is the cause of the back flow of blood into the atria from the ventricles? It could be damage of the
explanation: Atrioventricular valves (the bicuspid/mitral valve on the left and the tricuspid valve on the right) prevent the regurgitation (backflow) of blood from the ventricles into the atria during ventricular systole. Damage to these valves allows blood to leak backward into the atria.

topic: Structure and Function of Blood Vessels
prompt: The capillaries are blood vessels that have thin wall and large surface area since their function is
options: to return blood to the heart.
explanation: Capillaries have walls composed of a single layer of squamous endothelial cells (one cell thick) and form vast branching networks providing a huge total surface area. This minimizes diffusion distance and maximizes the rate of exchange of oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and metabolic wastes between blood and tissue cells.

topic: The Human Eye and Image Formation
prompt: During image formation, light is refracted twice before it is focused on the retina. This phenomenon happens at the
explanation: As light rays enter the eye, they undergo major refraction first at the curved air-cornea interface (fixed refraction) and a second adjustable refraction at the crystalline lens (fine-tuned via accommodation by ciliary muscles) to focus a sharp, inverted image onto the retina.

topic: Sense Organs: Interaction of Taste and Smell
prompt:
Three [Four] students designed the following experimental settings to understand the actual taste of a food.
Student 1: Blind folded two students, one of them tightly holding the nose while the other without holding the nose and tasting the food.
Student 2: Blind folded one student and the other left with open eyes, both holding their nose tightly while tasting the food.
Student 3: None of the participants blind folded and only one of them holding her nose tightly while tasting the food.
Student 4: None of the participants blind folded and both of them taste the food without holding the nose.
Which student designed the most appropriate experiment?
explanation: To isolate the true gustatory (taste) sensation and test the role of olfaction (smell) in flavor perception, visual cues must be controlled by blindfolding both participants, while varying only the independent variable (one holding the nose to block olfactory receptors vs. one with an open nose as control). Student 1 properly controlled sight and tested smell.

topic: Eye Defects and Corrections (Myopia)
prompt: Short sightedness is corrected by a concave lens because the problem arises due to a
options: weak eye lens that converges light slightly.
powerful eye lens that diverges light.
weak eye lens that diverges light.
strong eye lens that converges light too soon.
explanation: Short-sightedness (myopia) occurs when the eyeball is too long or the eye lens is too curved/strong (powerful), causing parallel light rays from distant objects to converge (focus) too soon in front of the retina. A diverging (concave) lens diverges the incoming rays slightly before they enter the eye so they focus directly on the retina.

topic: The Endocrine System (Hyperthyroidism)
prompt: A patient exhibited symptoms of weight loss, sweating, and irritability and the doctor suspected an endocrine malfunction that can be related to the
explanation: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine, which regulates the body's basal metabolic rate (BMR). Hyperthyroidism (oversecretion of thyroxine, as in Graves' disease) accelerates metabolism, resulting in rapid weight loss despite increased appetite, profuse sweating, heat intolerance, rapid heart rate, and nervousness/irritability.

topic: Endocrine vs. Exocrine Glands
prompt: Secretions of endocrine glands require receptors on cell membrane to be picked by their targets while exocrine secretions do not. This is because
options: exocrine glands secrete hormone directly to the blood stream.
exocrine glands are controlled by the nervous system.
explanation: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones directly into the bloodstream, which carries them throughout the entire body. To ensure hormones act only on specific target cells, target cells must possess specific complementary receptors. Exocrine glands, by contrast, deliver their secretions (e.g., enzymes, sweat, saliva) directly to a localized site via ducts.

topic: Classification of Viruses (DNA vs. RNA Viruses)
prompt: Which of the following diseases is caused by a DNA virus?
explanation: Cold sores are caused by the Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), which is a double-stranded DNA virus. By contrast, AIDS is caused by HIV (a retrovirus with an RNA genome), Swine flu is caused by H1N1 Influenza virus (an RNA virus), and COVID-19/Corona is caused by SARS-CoV-2 (an RNA virus).

topic: Resource Management and Recycling
prompt: Currently, natural resources are being depleted at increasing rate and waste materials are accumulated and discharged freely into water bodies. What is the best strategy to overcome these problems?
explanation: Recycling reprocesses waste materials into new usable products, which simultaneously reduces the extraction/depletion of virgin natural resources and prevents solid and chemical waste accumulation in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

topic: Biogeochemical Cycles (The Nitrogen Cycle)
prompt: Which stage of the nitrogen cycle needs the role of Rhizobium?
explanation: Rhizobium is a symbiotic bacterium living in the root nodules of leguminous plants (such as beans, peas, and clover) that catalyzes nitrogen fixation—the reduction of inert atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonium ions (NH₄⁺) usable by plants.

topic: Ecological Succession
prompt: A key aspect in the process of recovery of an ecosystem through succession is that
options: pioneer species always make the environment better.
higher organisms colonize the environment first.
a climax community of lichens and mosses is established at the end.
pioneer species always tend to be lower animals.
explanation: During ecological succession, hardy pioneer species (such as lichens and mosses in primary succession, or annual weeds in secondary succession) colonize harsh habitats first and modify the abiotic environment—weathering rock, building humus, increasing soil depth and nutrient/moisture retention—thereby making the environment more favorable ('better') for subsequent seral communities until a climax forest is reached.

topic: Terrestrial Biomes (Boreal Forest / Taiga)
prompt: What are the common plants of the boreal forest?
explanation: The boreal forest (taiga), located south of the Arctic tundra across northern North America and Eurasia, is dominated by cold-tolerant evergreen coniferous trees (conifers) such as spruce, fir, pine, and larch with needle-like leaves and waxy cuticles.

topic: Plant Hormones and Growth Regulation
prompt: Which one of the following may NOT be regulated by a plant hormone?
explanation: Plant hormones (phytohormones) regulate physiological processes: cytokinins regulate cell division, auxins and gibberellins regulate cell elongation, and ethylene regulates fruit ripening. Seed dispersal, however, is a physical/ecological process mediated by external agents such as wind, water, animals, or mechanical dehiscence.

topic: Apical Dominance and Pruning
prompt: Bushing of a plant results from
options: cancellation of the positive effect of apical dominance.
removal of the inhibitory effect of auxin.
decreased production of auxin by side shoots.
increased production of auxin by the main shoot.
explanation: Indole-3-acetic acid (auxin) synthesized at the apical (terminal) shoot tip diffuses downward and inhibits the outgrowth of lateral (axillary) buds—a phenomenon called apical dominance. Pruning or pinching off the shoot apex removes the source of this inhibitory auxin, allowing lateral buds to sprout and making the plant bushy.

topic: Biodiversity Conservation Methods
prompt: Actions such as protection of individual species, reduction of pollution, and reduction of deforestation can collectively be taken as methods of
explanation: Protecting endangered species, curbing habitat destruction (deforestation), and minimizing environmental pollution directly address the root causes of species loss and ecosystem degradation, collectively representing comprehensive biodiversity conservation strategies.

topic: Vegetation and Endemic/Indigenous Plants of Ethiopia
prompt: Which one of the following plants is NOT endemic to Ethiopia?
explanation: Mango (Mangifera indica) is an exotic fruit tree native to South Asia (India/Myanmar) that was introduced to Ethiopia. By contrast, Enset (Ensete ventricosum), Noug (Guizotia abyssinica), and Zigba (Podocarpus falcatus) are native/indigenous (or domesticated) Ethiopian flora highlighted in the national curriculum.

topic: National Parks and Wildlife of Ethiopia
prompt: Which one of the following national parks is characterized by the presence of wildlife such as elephant, lion, cheetah and giraffe?
explanation: Mago National Park (located in the lower Omo valley of southern Ethiopia) features savanna and acacia-commiphora bushland habitats that support large savanna mammals including African elephants, giraffes, lions, cheetahs, leopards, buffaloes, and zebras. Bale and Simien Mountains are Afro-alpine parks, and Awash National Park lacks giraffes and elephants.

topic: Invertebrate Phyla (Cnidaria / Coelenterata)
prompt: In kingdom animalia, which phylum poisons its prey by tentacles that contain stinging cells?
explanation: Members of the phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria)—such as Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemones, and corals—possess rings of tentacles armed with specialized stinging cells called cnidoblasts (nematocysts) that inject paralyzing toxins into prey.

topic: Kingdom Plantae (Division Bryophyta)
prompt: Mosses are grouped under division bryophyta because they
options: lack true root system and vascular tissue.
have true leaves, stems and roots.
are evergreen and photosynthesize all year round.
explanation: Bryophytes (mosses and liverworts) are non-vascular land plants: they lack specialized vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) and lack true roots, anchoring themselves instead via unicellular or multicellular hair-like rhizoids.

topic: Food Chains, Trophic Levels, and Ecological Pyramids
prompt: If you are asked to draw a pyramid of biomass of an aquatic habitat that contains zooplanktons, herrings, sea lions and phytoplankton, which organisms should be placed at the top of the pyramid?
explanation: In this marine food chain: Phytoplankton (primary producer, base) → Zooplankton (primary consumer) → Herrings (secondary consumer) → Sea lions (tertiary consumer / apex predator). The apex predator sits at the very top of the ecological pyramid.

topic: Plant Adaptations to Arid Environments (Xerophytes)
prompt: Which one of the following is an adaptation to reduce water loss in plants? Having
options: a single layered epidermis in leaves
explanation: A thick, waterproof waxy cuticle covering the leaf epidermis acts as a hydrophobic barrier that drastically reduces cuticular transpiration (evaporative water loss). Thin broad leaves and large open stomata increase water loss.

topic: Bergmann's Rule & Surface Area-to-Volume Ratio in Cold Climates
prompt: Why are arctic animals such as seals, walruses and whales large in body size? To
options: move in the water bodies easily
explanation: According to Bergmann's rule, endothermic animals in polar/arctic regions evolve large body sizes because a larger body has a smaller surface-area-to-volume ratio. Since heat is generated internally (proportional to volume) and lost across the skin (proportional to surface area), a small SA:V ratio minimizes heat loss to the freezing environment.

topic: Biological Research Institutes in Ethiopia (IBC/EBI)
prompt: The institute of biodiversity conservation is one of the biological research institutes of Ethiopia attempting to conserve the genetic resources of the country. As such, the institute's major research efforts focus on all of the following EXCEPT
explanation: The Institute of Biodiversity Conservation (IBC, now Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute - EBI) focuses on researching and conserving Ethiopia's living genetic resources—namely plants (forest, field crops, medicinal), animals, and microbial genetic resources. Physical soil conservation falls under agricultural/natural resource ministries rather than genetic biodiversity conservation.

topic: Microscopy and Staining Techniques
prompt: The importance of stains in microscopic investigations is explained by their effect in
explanation: Most biological cells and organelles are nearly transparent to light. Biological stains (dyes such as methylene blue, iodine, or haematoxylin) bind selectively to specific cellular structures (e.g., nuclei, cell walls, starch granules), creating color contrast against the background so they can be clearly distinguished.

topic: The Digestive System: Role of the Liver and Bile
prompt: One of the following problems can occur if the liver does NOT properly carry out its digestive functions.
explanation: The liver's primary digestive function is the production of bile, which contains bile salts that emulsify large dietary fat globules into tiny droplets (increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase) and sodium bicarbonate to neutralize acidic chyme. If liver bile production fails, fat emulsification is impaired, resulting in incomplete/partial digestion of fats.

topic: Chemical Digestion in the Stomach
prompt: Which of the following is the correct order of food substance, enzyme, and breakdown product of the digestive process in the stomach respectively?
explanation: In the acidic environment of the stomach (HCl, pH 1.5–2.5), chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which is activated to pepsin. Pepsin is a protease that hydrolyzes dietary proteins into shorter polypeptides/peptones (ultimately broken down to amino acids). None of the other options correctly pair substrate, enzyme, and product.

topic: Bell-Jar Lung Model and Mechanism of Breathing
prompt: Assume you are trying to demonstrate breathing movements using artificial lung and you pulled down the rubber sheet. This action of pulling represents which step of the actual breathing process?
options: Exhalation and contraction of the diaphragm
Inhalation and relaxation of the diaphragm
Inhalation and contraction of the diaphragm
Exhalation and relaxation of the diaphragm
explanation: In the bell-jar model of the respiratory system, the rubber sheet at the base represents the diaphragm. Pulling the rubber sheet downward simulates the contraction and flattening of the diaphragm muscle, which increases thoracic volume, lowers intrathoracic pressure below atmospheric pressure, and causes air to rush into the balloons (inhalation/inspiration).

topic: Lipids: Structure and Synthesis of Triglycerides
prompt: When three fatty acid molecules and a glycerol molecule undergo condensation reaction, they form
explanation: During lipid synthesis, three fatty acid molecules react via condensation (dehydration synthesis) with the three hydroxyl (-OH) groups of one glycerol molecule, releasing three water molecules and forming three covalent ester bonds to yield one triglyceride molecule.

topic: Phospholipid Bilayer Structure
prompt: In water, phospholipids become organized into a bilayer. In this configuration, which part of the bilayer faces towards the water?
explanation: Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules possessing a polar, hydrophilic (water-loving) phosphate head and two non-polar, hydrophobic (water-fearing) fatty acid hydrocarbon tails. In an aqueous environment, they spontaneously self-assemble into a bilayer with the hydrophilic phosphate heads facing outward toward the water on both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails tucked inside.

topic: Biochemical Food Tests (Emulsion and Grease-Spot Tests)
prompt:
Four students wanted to conduct chemical tests on unknown food particles and used the following chemicals and materials.
Student A: Test tubes and biuret solution
Student B: Test tubes, ethanol, water, filter paper
Student C: Test tubes, benedict's solution, water bath
Student D: Test tubes and iodine solution
Which of the above students planned a test for lipids?
explanation: Student B planned the two classic tests for lipids: the ethanol emulsion test (dissolving the sample in ethanol and pouring it into water to form a milky-white emulsion) and the translucent grease-spot test on filter paper. Student A tested for proteins (Biuret), Student C for reducing sugars (Benedict's), and Student D for starch (Iodine).

topic: Cofactors and Vitamin-Derived Coenzymes
prompt: Niacin is used to make the coenzyme
explanation: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) is an essential organic coenzyme derived from the vitamin niacin (Vitamin B₃ / nicotinic acid). Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) is derived from riboflavin (Vitamin B₂).

topic: Systematic Classification and Nomenclature of Enzymes (EC Classes)
prompt:
The following are reaction types catalyzed by different classes of enzymes.
1. Transferring hydrogen and oxygen atoms
2. Changing of the molecular form of the substrate
3. Joining of two molecules by the formation of new bonds
Which classes of enzymes catalyze the above reactions according to their consecutive order?
explanation: 1. Oxidoreductases catalyze redox reactions involving the transfer of hydrogen/oxygen atoms or electrons from one molecule to another. 2. Isomerases catalyze intramolecular rearrangements that change the structural/molecular form of a substrate into its isomer. 3. Ligases (synthetases) catalyze the joining of two molecules with the formation of new covalent bonds coupled to ATP hydrolysis.

topic: Oxidative Phosphorylation and Electron Transport Chain
prompt: The hydrogen ions that used to turn the rotor of ATP synthase come from
explanation: At the inner mitochondrial membrane, reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH₂ undergo oxidation (donating electrons and releasing H⁺ protons). As electrons pass down the electron transport chain, protons are pumped into the intermembrane space, creating the electrochemical proton gradient that drives H⁺ diffusion through the rotor of ATP synthase (chemiosmosis).

topic: Anaerobic Respiration and Lactic Acid Fermentation
prompt: What triggers fermentation during exercise?
options: Production of ATP beyond the cells demand
explanation: During vigorous muscle contraction, the demand for ATP exceeds the rate at which the cardiovascular and respiratory systems can deliver oxygen to muscle fibers. This shortage of oxygen halts the mitochondrial electron transport chain, triggering anaerobic lactic acid fermentation in the cytosol to regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue producing ATP.

topic: Biochemistry of Lactate Fermentation
prompt: Which of the following processes explains lactate production during anaerobic respiration in animal cells?
explanation: In animal cells under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate acts as the terminal hydrogen/electron acceptor and undergoes direct reduction by NADH (catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase) to form lactate (lactic acid) while regenerating oxidized NAD⁺. Unlike alcoholic fermentation in yeast, no decarboxylation occurs.

topic: Aerobic Respiration: The Link Reaction
prompt: Which one of the following descriptions holds true for the link reaction of respiration?
options: Pyruvate reacts with coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A
Glucose is converted to pyruvate through a chain of reactions
Hydrogen ion and ATP are synthesized
Reduced NAD and reduced FAD are produced
explanation: In the link reaction (oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix), the 3-carbon pyruvate molecule is decarboxylated (releasing CO₂), oxidized (reducing NAD⁺ to NADH), and combined with Coenzyme A to form the 2-carbon compound Acetyl Coenzyme A (Acetyl-CoA). No ATP or FADH₂ is produced in the link reaction.

topic: Theories of Evolution (Neo-Darwinism)
prompt: Which one of the following is the neo-Darwinian idea of evolution? Evolutionary changes occur due to
options: natural selection through genetics and behavior.
use and disuse of anatomical structures.
explanation: Neo-Darwinism (the Modern Synthetic Theory of Evolution) integrates Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection with modern Mendelian genetics, molecular biology (gene mutations, genetic recombination, allele frequencies in gene pools), and ethology (behavioral ecology) to explain how populations evolve.

topic: Human Evolution & Ethiopian Fossil Discoveries (Lucy / Dinknesh)
prompt: What is the significance of Australopithecus afarensis in the study of human evolution? To confirm
options: evolution of bipedalism before large brains
divergent evolution of Homo erectus from Homo habilis
true common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans
convergent evolution of Homo neanderthalensis and Homo erectus
explanation: The discovery of Australopithecus afarensis (such as the 3.2-million-year-old 'Lucy' / Dinknesh fossil in Hadar, Afar, Ethiopia) provided definitive paleontological proof that hominids evolved upright bipedal locomotion (pelvis, femur, and knee adapted for walking on two legs) millions of years before the evolution of a large cranial capacity (brain size ~400 cm³, similar to a chimpanzee).

topic: Innate / Instinctive Behaviour
prompt: Instinctive behavior
options: is common to all members of a species.
may be modified by new experiences.
explanation: Instinctive (innate) behavior is genetically programmed (hard-wired in the nervous system), present at birth, inflexible, and shared uniformly by all members of a species (species-specific) without requiring prior learning or experience.

topic: Learned Behaviour (Latent / Exploratory Learning)
prompt: Which one of the following statements is an example of latent learning?
options: The random movement of woodlice in response to changes in light intensity and humidity.
Knowledge of a mice about the immediate environment of its burrow may help it escape from predator.
Foraging bees returning from successful trip dance on the honey comb to recruit others to harvest a new.
Female baboon turns its buttock toward the dominant male to signify readiness to mate.
explanation: Latent (exploratory) learning occurs when an animal explores its surroundings and acquires a mental 'cognitive map' without any immediate reward or punishment; the learned knowledge remains hidden (latent) until a later survival need arises—such as a mouse using its prior knowledge of burrow pathways to quickly escape a predator.

topic: Enzyme Structure: Apoenzymes, Coenzymes, and Holoenzymes
prompt: Which one of the following is correct about the action of apoenzymes and coenzymes?
options: Coenzymes bind with cofactors to form an active enzyme.
Apoenzymes bind with enzymes to give catalytic activity.
Both apoenzymes and coenzymes combine with cofactors to form a non-active enzyme.
Coenzymes bind with enzymes [apoenzymes] to give catalytic activity.
explanation: An apoenzyme is the inactive protein portion of a conjugated enzyme, whereas a coenzyme is a non-protein organic molecule (often derived from vitamins). Neither is catalytically active alone; the coenzyme must bind to the enzyme (apoenzyme) to form a catalytically active holoenzyme.

topic: Comparison of Innate vs. Learned Behaviour
prompt:
Consider the following statements.
I. Genetically determined and common to all members of a species.
II. The behavior may be modified by new experiences.
III. Behavior is fully functional at the first attempt.
IV. Generally there is no modification of the behavior.
Which numbers describe innate and learned behaviors?
options: Innate: III, IV and Learned: I, II
Innate: I, II and Learned: III, IV
Innate: II, III, IV and Learned: I
Innate: I, III, IV and Learned: II
explanation: Innate behaviors are genetically determined and common to all members of a species (I), fully functional at the very first performance without practice (III), and rigid/unmodified over the organism's lifetime (IV). Learned behaviors are adaptive and modified through individual experience and practice (II).

topic: Social and Altruistic Behaviour in Animals
prompt: Which one of the following is an example of social behavior?
options: Exaggeration of size by fluffing up of feathers
Singing of frogs on spring nights
Caring for offspring that are not one's own
explanation: Caring for offspring that are not one's own (alloparental care / kin selection / altruism, such as worker bees nursing the queen's larvae or helper meerkats guarding pups) is a hallmark of complex cooperative social behavior. Options A and C describe agonistic/territorial behavior, and Option B describes courtship behavior.

topic: Mechanism of Enzyme Action & Transition-State Intermediate
prompt:
Consider the following reaction.
Reactant A + Reactant B + Enzyme → Intermediate → Product AB + Enzyme
At which point are the chemical bonds weakened? At the
explanation: When substrates (Reactants A and B) bind to the active site of an enzyme, they form an unstable Enzyme-Substrate (ES) complex / transition-state intermediate. In this intermediate state, conformational changes put physical and electronic strain on existing chemical bonds, weakening them and lowering the activation energy needed to form Product AB.

topic: Models of Enzyme Action (Induced-Fit Model)
prompt: How do enzymes bind and act on their substrates? By using the
options: lock-and-key model and reducing energy of the substrate
induced-fit model and providing extra energy for the substrate
lock-and-key model and changing themselves into products
induced-fit model and putting the substrates under tension
explanation: According to Koshland's induced-fit model, the active site of an enzyme is flexible and molds itself tightly around the substrate upon binding. This conformational adjustment puts the substrate's chemical bonds under physical tension/strain, pushing it toward the transition state and lowering the activation energy of the reaction.

topic: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity and Denaturation
prompt: Which of the following external factors influence the turnover rate of enzymes by completely damaging their tertiary structure?
explanation: Extreme high temperatures (excess kinetic thermal energy breaking hydrogen and hydrophobic bonds) and extreme pH levels (H⁺/OH⁻ ions disrupting ionic bonds and disulfide bridges) cause irreversible denaturation—completely unfolding and destroying the 3D globular tertiary structure and active site of the enzyme.

topic: Indigenous Biotechnology: Fermentation of Teff Dough (Injera)
prompt: During baking of injera, the CO₂ produced by yeast is used to
options: increase the shelf life of injera.
explanation: During the fermentation of teff batter by yeasts (such as Saccharomyces species) and lactic acid bacteria, carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas is evolved. When the batter is poured onto the hot mitad, escaping CO₂ bubbles rise and burst, leavening the batter and creating the characteristic spongy, porous 'eyes' (ethiopian: ayen) texture of injera.

topic: The Nervous System: Synaptic Transmission
prompt: The nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another by a neurotransmitter at the
explanation: A synapse is the microscopic functional junction (containing the synaptic cleft) between the axon terminal of a presynaptic neuron and the dendrite or cell body of a postsynaptic neuron. Chemical neurotransmitters (such as acetylcholine) diffuse across the synaptic cleft to transmit the nerve impulse from one neuron to the next.

topic: Action Potential and Depolarization of an Axon
prompt: What happens if the axon is stimulated? Formation of
options: negative charge in both sides of the axon
positive charge outside of the axon
explanation: At rest, an axon is polarized with a negative charge inside (-70 mV) and a positive charge outside. When stimulated past threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and sodium ions (Na⁺) rush rapidly into the axoplasm, reversing the membrane potential so that a positive charge (+40 mV) forms inside the axon (depolarization).

topic: Reflex Arc and the Patellar (Knee-Jerk) Reflex
prompt: Assume you wanted to demonstrate a simple reflex action using the knee jerk reflex. You asked a friend to sit with one leg crossed over the other. Which one of the following indicates the correct demonstration?
options: Pulling down your friend's leg that is followed by downward movement
Hitting your friend on the toes followed by sudden upward movement of the leg
Bending up your friend's leg followed by downward movement of the leg
Hitting your friend below the knee cap followed by a sudden upward movement
explanation: To elicit the patellar (knee-jerk) stretch reflex, the patellar tendon just below the kneecap (patella) is tapped briskly. This stretches the quadriceps femoris muscle spindle receptors, sending an impulse via a sensory neuron to the spinal cord and directly back via a motor neuron to contract the quadriceps, causing a sudden upward/forward kick of the lower leg.

topic: Modes of Natural Selection (Disruptive Selection)
prompt: A finch with an average length beak was not able to obtain insects out of the cracks in the bark of trees as well as one with a longer beak. It was also not able to crush seeds as well as one with a shorter beak. Over time, those with the longer beaks and those with the shorter beaks increased in numbers, while those with average length beaks decreased in number. Which type of selection has been operated in this scenario?
explanation: Disruptive (diversifying) selection favors individuals at both extremes of a phenotypic distribution (both very short beaks and very long beaks) while selecting against individuals with the intermediate/average phenotype, resulting in a bimodal distribution and potentially driving sympatric speciation.

topic: Anatomy and Function of the Human Ear
prompt:
This item is based on the following diagram of the human ear.
[See Embedded Diagram]
What is the name of the human ear part represented by letter 'F' in the above diagram?
explanation: In the diagram of the human ear, letter 'F' points directly to the snail-shell-shaped spiral tube of the inner ear known as the cochlea. The fluid-filled cochlea houses the Organ of Corti, which contains mechanoreceptor hair cells that transduce sound vibrations into auditory nerve impulses.

topic: The Cell Theory (Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow)
prompt: The cell theory states that cells
options: contain different organelles with no specialization.
come from pre-existing cells by division.
explanation: The three core tenets of Modern Cell Theory state that: (1) all living organisms are composed of one or more cells; (2) the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; and (3) all cells arise only from pre-existing cells by cell division (Rudolf Virchow's 'Omnis cellula e cellula').

topic: Chromosomal Mutations (Translocation / Deletion in Leukemia)
prompt: Which type of chromosome mutation causes leukemia?
explanation: Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML) is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome abnormality involving chromosomes 9 and 22 (originally thought to be a simple deletion on chromosome 22, later shown to be a reciprocal translocation/insertion creating the BCR-ABL oncogene, while certain acute leukemias involve chromosomal deletions/translocations). Note: In the Ethiopian Grade 12 textbook, leukemia (CML) is discussed under chromosomal mutations—specifically reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (or partial deletion/insertion depending on the exam key's classification of the shortened chromosome 22). Both Deletion [D] and Insertion/Translocation [B] are discussed in exam keys; we highlight the exact textbook mechanism.

topic: Theories on the Origin of Life (Eternity of Life)
prompt: Which theory of the origin of life states that life has no beginning or ending?
explanation: The Eternity of Life (steady-state) theory proposes that the universe and life have always existed without beginning or end, and that life is eternal and unchanging in its fundamental existence.

topic: Lines of Evidence for Evolution (Paleontology)
prompt: Which one of the following is paleontological evidence of evolution?
options: The presence of homologous structures in living organisms
Traces of organisms from the remote past
Similarities in the DNA base sequences of different organisms
Similarities in the development of embryos in different organisms
explanation: Paleontology is the study of fossils—the preserved remains, casts, impressions, or traces of organisms that lived in the remote geological past. Option A is comparative anatomy, Option C is comparative biochemistry, and Option D is comparative embryology.

topic: Ultrastructure of the Chloroplast & Sites of Photosynthesis
prompt:
This item is based on the diagram of a chloroplast given below.
[See Embedded Diagram]
In the above diagram of the chloroplast, what are the sites of the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis respectively?
explanation: In the chloroplast diagram, pointer '1' indicates the fluid-filled matrix called the stroma, while pointer '2' indicates a stack of thylakoids (granum). The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes/grana (2), and the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma (1). Therefore, the respective order is 2 and 1.

topic: Sex-Linked Inheritance (Red-Green Colour Blindness)
prompt: A colour blind daughter can be born when the
options: mother is colour blind and the father is normal.
father is colour blind and the mother is normal.
mother is carrier and the father is colour blind.
father is normal and the mother is carrier.
explanation: Red-green colour blindness is an X-linked recessive trait (Xᶜ). For a female (XX) to be colour blind (XᶜXᶜ), she must inherit one recessive Xᶜ allele from her mother and one recessive Xᶜ allele from her father. This occurs when the father is colour blind (XᶜY) and the mother is either a carrier (XᴺXᶜ) or colour blind (XᶜXᶜ). Among the choices, 'mother is carrier and the father is colour blind' gives a 50% probability of a daughter being colour blind.

topic: Asexual Reproduction / Vegetative Propagation by Stem Cuttings
prompt: A farmer cut off several regions of a stem near to the buds of a plant. He removed some of the leaves and dipped the cuts end in some hormones rooting powder and planted the cuttings in a compost. He kept the cuttings well watered and within a few weeks they developed their own root system and became new independent plants. Which one of the following is correct about this experiment? The new plants are most probably
options: phenotypically and genotypically different from the parent plant and from each other.
genetically and phenotypically identical to the parent plant and to each other.
phenotypically identical but genetically different from each other.
genotypically identical but phenotypically different from the parent.
explanation: Propagating plants via stem cuttings is a method of artificial vegetative propagation (asexual reproduction) relying solely on mitotic cell division. Because no meiosis or fertilization takes place, all offspring are clones—genetically and phenotypically identical to the single parent plant and to one another.

topic: Molecular Genetics: Semi-Conservative DNA Replication
prompt: During DNA replication
options: DNA helicase transports nucleotides that are used to build the new DNA.
the base sequence in the new DNA will be slightly changed from the parent DNA.
DNA polymerase assembles new nucleotides into a new strand.
the parent DNA will become different from the daughter DNA.
explanation: During semi-conservative DNA replication, DNA helicase unwinds and unzips the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds, while DNA polymerase catalyzes the covalent joining (assembly) of free complementary deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) along each template strand to synthesize identical new daughter DNA strands.

topic: Nature of the Genetic Code (Degeneracy)
prompt: With four different bases to work with, there are 64 possible triplet codes, but only 20 amino acids are used to make all the different proteins. This is because the DNA code is
explanation: The genetic code is described as degenerate (redundant) because there are 64 possible triplet codons (4³ = 64, of which 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons) for only 20 standard amino acids—meaning that most amino acids are specified by more than one triplet codon.

topic: Protein Synthesis: Translation Termination (Stop Codons)
prompt: If mRNA brings the code 'UGA' into the ribosome
options: translation ceases and protein synthesis terminates.
tRNA will bring the amino acid methionine.
explanation: In mRNA, the three triplet codons UAA, UAG, and UGA are nonsense or 'stop' (termination) codons. No tRNA molecule has an anticodon complementary to UGA; instead, protein release factors bind to the A-site of the ribosome, causing the completed polypeptide chain to detach and terminating translation.

topic: Reproductive System and Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle
prompt: Breakdown of the thick spongy wall of the uterus at the end of the menstrual cycle is associated with the
options: decrease in progesterone and estrogen concentration.
increase in oestrogen and progesterone concentration.
explanation: If fertilization and implantation do not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates around day 26–28 of the menstrual cycle. This causes a sharp drop (decrease) in blood progesterone and oestrogen concentrations, depriving the thickened endometrium of hormonal support and triggering menstruation (shedding of the uterine lining).

topic: Progression of HIV/AIDS & Acute Seroconversion Window
prompt: The first incubation period of HIV is characterized by a duration of
options: 20 years before all the symptoms appear in well-nourished people.
3–12 weeks when mild symptoms are manifested.
2–3 years for the progress of infection to AIDS.
explanation: Following initial HIV infection, the primary acute phase / seroconversion period occurs within 3 to 12 weeks (typically 2–6 weeks), during which viral replication spikes, mild flu-like symptoms (fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes) may appear, and anti-HIV antibodies begin to reach detectable levels.

topic: Homeostasis and Thermoregulation (Physiological vs. Behavioural)
prompt: Which one of the following is a behavioral method of temperature regulation in homoiotherms?
explanation: Thermoregulatory mechanisms are divided into physiological (autonomic) and behavioral responses. Piloerection and vasodilation are involuntary physiological responses. Aestivation (summer dormancy in burrows/shade to escape extreme heat and drought) and bathing/clothing/seeking shade are behavioral methods of temperature regulation in homoiotherms (note: licking fur/panting is also an evaporative cooling behavior in some mammals, while aestivation is explicitly listed under behavioral methods in the Ethiopian Grade 10 Biology textbook Table of Thermoregulation).

topic: Homeostasis: Osmoregulation and ADH Negative Feedback
prompt: What will happen if the water content of the blood is too high?
options: The second coiled tubule of the kidney becomes more permeable.
Osmoreceptors stimulate pituitary gland to release ADH.
The kidney reabsorbs more water back into the blood.
explanation: When blood water content is too high (low blood osmolarity), hypothalamic osmoreceptors inhibit the posterior pituitary gland, causing Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) secretion to decrease. With less ADH, the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct walls become less permeable to water, less water is reabsorbed into the blood, and a large volume of dilute urine is excreted.

topic: Transport in Plants: Transpiration Pull and Cohesion-Tension Theory
prompt: The movement of water from the roots up to the top leaves of tall trees is carried out by
options: loss of water by transpiration and its replacement by osmosis.
active transport in the roots and osmosis in the leaves.
the low cohesive and adhesive forces of water in the xylem.
active transport in both the roots and leaves.
explanation: Water ascends tall trees passively via the transpiration stream (cohesion-tension mechanism): evaporation of water vapor from leaf mesophyll cells through stomata (transpiration) lowers water potential in the leaves, pulling a continuous column of water upward through the xylem (held together by high cohesion and adhesion) and drawing water into root hairs from the soil by osmosis.

topic: The Scientific Method and Structure of a Scientific Report
prompt: From the following options, which one contains the steps of writing a scientific report in the correct order?
options: Title → Prediction → Hypothesis → Procedure → Evaluation → Conclusion → Results → Acknowledgement
Title → Hypothesis → Prediction → Procedure → Results → Conclusion → Evaluation → Acknowledgement
Title → Hypothesis → Prediction → Evaluation → Results → Procedure → Conclusion → Acknowledgement
Title → Hypothesis → Procedure → Prediction → Results → Conclusion → Evaluation → Acknowledgement
explanation: As taught in Grade 11 Biology Unit 1, the standard logical sequence for writing a formal scientific investigation report is: Title → Hypothesis (or Introduction/Aim) → Prediction → Procedure (Materials & Methods) → Results (Data Presentation) → Conclusion → Evaluation (Assessing reliability/errors) → Acknowledgement (and References).

topic: Biological Laboratory Tools: Principles of Centrifugation
prompt: What type of force is responsible if a stool solution is placed in a centrifuge, spins the tube at high speed and the solid particles are forced to settle down at the bottom?
explanation: A centrifuge spins samples at high rotational speeds to generate an artificial sedimenting force (measured in Relative Centrifugal Force, RCF, or ×g—multiples of Earth's gravitational force) while the tube walls exert inward centripetal force. Note: In the Ethiopian Grade 11 textbook, centrifugation is described as using ultra-high-speed rotation to vastly amplify gravitational force (or centripetal/centrifugal force depending on the curriculum key). Both Gravitational force [D] (via 'g-force' sedimentation) and Centripetal force [C] (the circular motion physics term) are explained in detail in the guide.

topic: Steps of the Scientific Method (Observation & Asking a Question)
prompt: Ten percent of attendants of a wedding ceremony were sick just after having lunch at the ceremony. What should a student do first to prove scientifically that the sickness was actually linked to the food eaten at the ceremony? She should
options: give drugs to the sick individuals before they contaminate others.
take food sample to a laboratory and analyze the presence of toxin.
ask herself why ten percent of the attendants were sick.
take stool sample of the sick individuals and analyze the presence of toxins.
explanation: In the scientific method, after making an initial observation (10% of wedding guests fell ill after lunch), the very first scientific step is to formulate a clear research question ('Ask herself why ten percent of the attendants became sick'), which then leads to background research, forming a hypothesis, and testing it via laboratory analysis (Options B and D).

topic: Biological Importance and Properties of Water (Viscosity)
prompt: Which one of the following importance of water is directly related with its ideal viscosity?
explanation: Water has a low, ideal viscosity that allows it to flow smoothly through narrow biological tubes—such as blood capillaries in animals and xylem/phloem vessels in plants—making it an ideal transport medium for dissolved nutrients, gases, and wastes (and allowing aquatic organisms to swim with minimal resistance).

topic: Thermal Properties of Water (Latent Heat of Vaporization)
prompt: Which property of water prevents ponds from drying during the long dry season? High
explanation: Because of extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules, water has a very high latent heat of vaporization—meaning a large amount of heat energy is required to convert liquid water into water vapor. This slows down evaporation and prevents ponds, lakes, and rivers from rapidly drying up during hot dry seasons.

topic: Comparison of Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells
prompt:
The following table compares prokaryotes and eukaryotes:
Feature | Prokaryotes | Eukaryotes
DNA | X | Linear
Mitochondria | Absent | Y
Ribosomes | Present (70S) | Z
Cell membrane | Present | Present
In the above table, X, Y, and Z can be respectively stated as
explanation: Prokaryotic cells possess circular naked DNA (X = Circular), whereas eukaryotic cells possess membrane-bound mitochondria (Y = Present) and larger cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes (Z = Present (80S)). Thus X, Y, Z are Circular, present, present (80S).

topic: Functions of the Plasma Membrane vs. Mitochondria
prompt: Which one of the following is NOT the function of the plasma membrane in eukaryotic cells?
options: Isolating the cell from the external environment
Transferring chemical energy from carbohydrates to ATP
explanation: In eukaryotic cells, transferring chemical energy from carbohydrates into ATP (aerobic cellular respiration / oxidative phosphorylation) takes place inside the mitochondria, NOT at the outer plasma membrane. Isolating the cell, selective material exchange, and cell signaling via membrane receptors are all core plasma membrane functions.

topic: Fluid Mosaic Model of the Plasma Membrane
prompt: Which one of the following is correct with respect to the structural components of the plasma membrane?
options: Integral proteins are found inserted in the lipid bilayer.
Peripheral proteins are located outside the lipid bilayer.
Channel proteins cover the outer layer of the lipid bilayer.
Glycoproteins are found on the cytoplasmic side of the cell membrane.
explanation: In Singer and Nicolson's Fluid Mosaic Model, integral (intrinsic) proteins have hydrophobic regions that penetrate partially or completely through the phospholipid bilayer (transmembrane proteins, including channel and carrier proteins). Glycoproteins face the extracellular exterior (forming the glycocalyx), not the cytoplasmic side.

topic: Osmosis, Water Potential, and Plasmolysis in Plant Tissues
prompt: Suppose three potato cylinders were kept in 25%, 15% and 5% sucrose solution respectively and a fourth cylinder was placed in distilled water. Which of the cylinders will be more flaccid? The cylinder in
explanation: The 25% sucrose solution is the most hypertonic (lowest/most negative water potential) relative to the potato cell sap. Consequently, the steepest water potential gradient exists between the potato cells and the 25% sucrose solution, causing the greatest net efflux of water by osmosis, severe plasmolysis, and the most flaccid potato cylinder.

topic: Osmotic Effects on Animal Cells (Crenation and Haemolysis)
prompt:
Consider the following table which shows a result of an experiment where red blood cells were placed in three different solutions X, Y and Z.
Solutions | Changes observed on RBCs
X | Shrink
Y | Burst
Z | No change
The three different solutions in which the blood cells were placed in order of X, Y, Z were
explanation: In Solution X, RBCs shrink (crenate) because water leaves the cells by osmosis into a hypertonic solution. In Solution Y, RBCs swell and burst (haemolyse) because water enters the cells by osmosis from a hypotonic solution. In Solution Z, there is no net water movement or shape change because the solution is isotonic.

topic: Concept and Levels of Biodiversity (Genetic, Species, and Ecosystem)
prompt: A more comprehensive definition of biodiversity can be given as the
options: richness, ecological and genetic variability of species.
number of individuals of a species in a given area.
diversity of plants and animals in a given area.
number of individuals of a given animal species.
explanation: Biodiversity encompasses three interconnected hierarchical levels: species richness/diversity (variety of all living species, including microbes, fungi, plants, and animals), genetic variability within each species, and ecological/ecosystem variability across habitats.

topic: Population Dynamics and Carrying Capacity (Sigmoid Growth Curve)
prompt: At which stage of the population growth curve is the rate of natality and the rate of mortality are expected to be equal?
explanation: During the stationary (plateau) phase of a population growth curve, the population has reached the environment's carrying capacity (K). Limiting factors balance reproductive output so that the birth rate (natality) equals the death rate (mortality), resulting in zero net population growth.

topic: Population Regulation: Intraspecific vs. Interspecific Competition
prompt: Identify the correct statement about intra-specific competition? It is a competition
options: of two species inhabiting the same ecological area.
that leads to local extinction of the species.
explanation: Intraspecific competition occurs between members of the exact same species living in the same habitat. Because conspecific individuals occupy the exact same ecological niche, they compete intensely for all types of requirements—identical food sources, water, territory/nesting sites, light, and mates.

topic: Model Organisms in Genetics (Thomas Hunt Morgan & Fruit Flies)
prompt: Why Drosophila melanogaster are considered ideal for genetic experiments? Because they
options: have the highest number of chromosomes.
breed and keep in large numbers easily.
complete their life cycle within one month.
explanation: The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster is an ideal genetic model organism because it is small, inexpensive to culture, easy to breed and keep in large numbers in laboratory vials, produces hundreds of offspring per mating, has a very short life cycle (~10–14 days, not one month), and has only 4 pairs of chromosomes (2n = 8).

topic: Meiosis and Sources of Genetic Variation
prompt: Which one of the following statements best describes the mechanisms by which meiosis brings about variation? Variation in meiosis is because of
options: variations in the content of the cytoplasm between the cells.
reduction division that leads to haploid cell formation.
explanation: Meiosis generates genetic variation among gametes through two principal mechanisms: (1) Crossing over (chiasmata formation and reciprocal exchange of chromatid segments between homologous chromosomes during Prophase I), and (2) Independent assortment (random orientation of homologous chromosome pairs at the equatorial plate during Metaphase I).

topic: Photorespiration in C₃ Plants
prompt: In the tropical regions, where there is higher temperature, which one of the following is most likely to take place in the C₃ plants? Rubisco binds with
options: O₂ to produce GP and phosphoglycolate.
CO₂ to produce glucose and water.
explanation: In hot, dry tropical environments, C₃ plants close their stomata to conserve water, causing internal CO₂ levels to drop and O₂ levels to rise. Under high temperatures and low CO₂:O₂ ratios, the active site of RuBisCO binds with O₂ instead of CO₂ (oxygenation of RuBP), producing one molecule of 3-carbon GP (glycerate-3-phosphate) and one molecule of 2-carbon phosphoglycolate in the wasteful process of photorespiration.

topic: The Calvin Cycle (Light-Independent Reactions)
prompt: During the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis
options: glucose is directly produced from GP.
RuBP reacts with CO₂ to directly form TP.
some of the GP is used to regenerate RuBP.
GP is reduced to TP by reduced NADP.
explanation: In the Calvin cycle: (1) CO₂ combines with 5C RuBP to form an unstable 6C intermediate that immediately splits into two molecules of 3C GP (glycerate-3-phosphate); (2) GP is then reduced to 3C TP (triose phosphate) using energy from ATP and hydrogen/electrons from reduced NADP (NADPH) generated in the light-dependent reactions; (3) Five out of every six TP molecules (not GP directly) are used to regenerate RuBP, and one-sixth exits to form hexose/glucose.

topic: Structure and Function of Photosystems in Thylakoid Membranes
prompt: The suitability of the structural arrangement of a chloroplast in relation to its function can be indicated by the fact that
options: all pigments are floating around the solution of the stroma.
all pigments in the photosystem are linked to the electron transport chain.
carotenoids are used as a reaction center from which electrons are excited.
the different pigments absorb the same wavelength.
explanation: Within the thylakoid membranes, photosynthetic pigments (chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, and carotenoids) are precisely organized into light-harvesting antenna complexes (photosystems) that funnel absorbed photon energy to the chlorophyll a reaction center, which is directly coupled to the electron transport chain in the membrane.

topic: Alternative Carbon Fixation Pathways (CAM Plants)
prompt: Which one of the following events occurs during the day time in the CAM photosynthetic pathway?
options: The stomata open to allow CO₂.
explanation: In Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM) plants (such as cacti and pineapples), stomata open only at night to fix CO₂ into oxaloacetate and store it as malate (malic acid) in vacuoles. During the daytime, stomata close to prevent water loss, and malate is transported out of the vacuoles and decarboxylated to release CO₂, which enters the Calvin cycle using ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions.

topic: Stoichiometry of the Calvin Cycle
prompt: How many turns of the light independent reaction cycle are required to make one molecule of triose phosphate?
explanation: Each single turn of the Calvin cycle fixes 1 molecule of CO₂ (1 carbon atom). To achieve a net gain of one 3-carbon Triose Phosphate (TP / G3P) molecule that can leave the cycle (while regenerating the three 5-carbon RuBP acceptor molecules from the remaining five TP molecules), 3 molecules of CO₂ must be fixed—requiring 3 turns of the Calvin cycle (and 6 turns to synthesize one 6-carbon glucose molecule).
